rows.evidence: Q1: Sec 2 - primary survey of 131 drip-adopter households in Pokharathok village (Palpa, Nepal) in 2003 using unstructured questionnaires, random-spot time observation, focus groups and a benefit-cost analysis. Q2: Sec 3.2 - own data analysis indicates that before drip 72% of farmers ate no vegetables at meals, whereas after the intervention 100% of drip users consumed vegetables with meals; about 30% bought milking cows from vegetable income so milk products entered meals; Table 2 - two-thirds of women agreed drip changed daily vegetable intake; Box 1 case of a de facto female-headed household ensuring food security. Q4: Table 5 and Sec 3.2/3.3 - the study quantifies the intermediate pathway: vegetable output per household (about 510 kg), gross household income (about US$67), and women's newly gained access to and control of that income (92% had no income source before), which is linked to food purchases. Q6: Secs 2 and 3.2 - the effect is reported at community level across 131 adopter households in one village, with a village-wide boom in vegetable production and collection centres, not a single plot. Q7: Sec 3.3 and 3.4 - authors state from their findings that vegetables are grown only where irrigation water is available, that income generation is not possible unless a reliable and sustained output market exists, and that access to water, market sustenance and credit access are crucial; Sec 4 - benefits realised when the technology is offered within a favourable institutional environment. Q8: Sec 4 - the long-term sustainability of the livelihood is questionable, returns depend on market prices and the number of adopters, and the degree to which outside institutional support made the technology viable is not known.
rows.notes: Q3 'no': dietary change is based entirely on self-reported recall in interviews and group discussions; participant observation was used only for time allocation, so there is no independent measurement of consumption. Q5 'no': one village, one agro-ecology. Q9 'no': results are percentages of respondents and mean values with no SD, CI or range for the dietary/food-security result; the '1-2 hours' and rent ranges concern other variables. Note the before/after design has no control group and the income-increase figure (>50%) is attributed to Gurung (2000), not the study's own data.

rows.evidence: Q1: Sec 2 - primary household survey (n=131), focus groups, time-allocation observation and benefit-cost analysis in a West Nepal village, 2003. Q2: Sec 3.3 and Table 5 - the study's own benefit-cost analysis of drum-kit drip vegetable farming gives gross household income of about US$67 per 0.0127 ha plot, NPV US$16.1, BCR 2.4, IRR about 38% and payback 1.6 years, indicating financial viability; Sec 3.2 - 92% of women had no income source before adoption and now have access to and control over vegetable income, Dalits and de facto female-headed households gaining; Table 2 - 84% agree drip generates more income than other livelihood options; Sec 3.2 - women formed self-help saving-credit groups accumulating over NRs 100,000 and widened social networks. Q4: Table 5 and Sec 3.3 - the income pathway is quantified through measured vegetable production (510 kg/household), revenue, labour, rent and input costs. Q6: Sec 2/3.2 - results are reported for the adopter community of 131 households in the village, including village-level marketing through collection centres, i.e. above the single plot. Q7: Sec 3.3 - authors state that income generation is not possible unless a reliable and sustained output market is established, that profitability for landless/renting farmers holds provided credit is available at reasonable terms, and that access to water plus market and credit support are crucial; Sec 3.4 - expansion is difficult where water is scarce. Q8: Sec 4 - authors state that long-term sustainability of the livelihood is questionable, returns depend partly on market prices which are a function of the number of adopters, and the degree to which outside institutional support made the technology viable is not known.
rows.notes: The passage itself is about income and poverty reduction; the study's own evidence on this is a before/after survey and a BCA from self-reported production and cost figures, with no control group. Q3 'no': the perception survey and the BCA both draw on the same household interviews, so they are not independent methods. Q5 'no': single village. Q9 'no': no SD, CI or range is given for income, NPV, BCR or IRR (only a range for land rent, an input). The >50% increase in mean vegetable income is cited from Gurung (2000), not the study's own result. The 'social_cohesion' function is only loosely matched: the study does report self-help groups and expanded social networks but the rated passage concerns income/poverty.

notes: The document is IWMI Working Paper 87 (Upadhyay, Samad and Giordano, 2005), whereas the citation is given as Upadhyay and Samad 2004; the content matches the cited topic. Tables 1-7 and the reference list are rendered in a corrupted font encoding and could not be read directly; table values were taken from the surrounding text where stated. Single-village case study with before/after recall data, no comparison group, no dispersion statistics.
